basis: Written from the published specification and established practice in the field; no new sources were read. Unreviewed.

distinguishingFeatures: Models the continuity capability across BIA, plans, exercises and activations, not the incident itself.
Keeps impact tolerance, objectives, plan, invocation, restoration and return to normal as separate.
Treats readiness as evidenced by exercises rather than by having a plan.
References people, sites, systems and suppliers held in their own masters.

may: Compile business impact analysis inputs from dependency data.
Check plans for stale contacts, owners and dependencies.
Run tabletop exercise scripts and record findings.
Track recovery tasks during an activation and report status.
mustNot: Activate or stand down a continuity plan without authority.
Accept residual risk on behalf of the organisation.
Disclose protected continuity details such as site layouts or key personnel.
Report recovery objectives as met without test evidence.
Start failover actions in production during an exercise without approval.
requiresHuman: Plan activation and return to normal operations.
Setting recovery objectives and impact tolerances.

considerations: Continuity plans protect people's safety and essential services, not only revenue.
Plans must consider staff wellbeing during disruptions, not only availability.
Prioritisation of services decides who is served first in a crisis.
affectedParties: Customers and communities depending on services

items: A continuity capability has a scope, an owner, BIA results, recovery objectives, plans and exercise records.
It is confused with incident response, disaster recovery of one system or a risk register.
Failed recovery because plans were never tested.
Harm to people when critical services stop longer than tolerated.
Misuse of leaked plans to target weak points.
ISO/IEC 27031 ICT readiness for business continuity.
